absent: Grace-period lifecycle, quiescent-state reporting, tree traversal and node locking are not shown.
Segmented callback enqueue, advancement, and invocation helpers beyond layout are not shown.
Stall detection, warning emission, and notifier chain management beyond stub return codes are not shown.
Grace coordinator transitions, waiting and wakeup protocol beyond the idle test are not shown.
Dereference primitives and full ordering rules beyond publication are not shown.
Build-time selection among fanout and level alternatives and values of configuration inputs are not shown.
Poison marker values, validity checks, and bit-lock and nulls termination protocols beyond use sites are not shown.

findings.text: Tree fanout is configurable with documented fallbacks. Internal levels use a build configuration value when present and otherwise fall back to sixty four in one alternative and thirty two in another. Leaf level uses a configuration value when present and otherwise sixteen.

Per-level capacities form a multiplicative chain rooted at leaf capacity. Each higher threshold multiplies the previous threshold by the internal fanout, yielding four successive capacities used to size the tree.

Supported tree depth ranges from one to four levels. The root layer always holds one node. Deeper layers size each level by rounding up the configured CPU count divided by the matching capacity threshold, with upper layers using larger capacities. Total node count is the sum across layers and an initializer list mirrors the per-layer counts from root to leaf.

Each level has two diagnostic names, one for the combining node and one for its force-quiescent counterpart. Names follow a numeric suffix pattern starting at zero and extending with depth, with one entry per level in root to leaf order.
Stall notification distinguishes two causes with small integer codes. Normal stalls use value one and expedited stalls use value two.

In the routed configuration the stall chain registration helpers are inert inline shims. Registration always reports an already-present failure and unregistration always reports a missing-entry failure, with no observable state change.

The simple callback list carries a head link to the first callback, an indirect tail anchor for the place where the next callback attaches, and a signed length count. Its static initializer describes an empty list with no head and the tail anchored at the head field.

Segmented callback lists use four ordered segments indexed zero through three for done, wait, next-ready and next. The total segment count is four, and each boundary serves both as the tail of one stage and the head of the following stage.

The segmented list holds a head link, one tail anchor per segment, one grace sequence value per segment, a total length plus one length per segment, and a flag byte. Total length is atomic in offload builds and plain otherwise. Flag bit zero means enabled and bit one means offloaded. Its initializer starts empty with every tail anchored at the head.

The grace coordinator holds an integer state, a count field, a wait queue for waiters, and a callback head for deferred work. Static initialization zeroes the state and count and prepares the wait queue, and a helper macro defines a named instance with that initialization.
Idle is defined as coordinator state zero observed with a single volatile read. The predicate warns under lock checking when invoked outside any reader context, indicating suspicious use.

The lock checking helper has two build variants. When checking is active it keeps a per-site already-warned flag in unlikely data and reports at most once when debugging is enabled and the supplied condition holds. When inactive it has no effect and only mentions the condition in an unevaluated context.
The any-reader-held test reports true exactly when the current context is non-preemptible, serving as a conservative proxy for holding some read-side critical section.

Pointer publication provides release ordering so prior initialization becomes visible before the pointer itself, with address-space annotation for checking. Compile-time null values use a plain volatile store while other values use a release store, preserving ordering without extra cost for clearing.

Doubly linked traversal exposes forward and backward pointer views, single volatile reads for entries, null-returning first and next helpers, and loop forms that walk forward until returning to the head. Entry conversion derives the enclosing object from a sampled link. Lockless entry forms also use single volatile reads but carry no reader requirement.

Single-headed hash list traversal exposes first, next and back-pointer views with volatile and checked dereference forms. Loop forms iterate until a null link, with variants for plain readers, bottom-half readers, non-tracing readers, sleepable readers with an explicit lock condition, plus continue and resume-from-current forms.

Bit-locked hash lists expose first and next views where the first word carries lock bits, plus a dereference helper that validates lock state and masks those bits to obtain the node pointer, with forward loops and continue forms built on raw dereference. Nulls-terminated lists expose first, next and back-pointer views in the same style.

List and hash-list entry loops optionally accept a caller-supplied lock condition. Checking builds warn when neither that condition nor any reader context is held for plain variants, or when the supplied sleepable-lock condition is absent for sleepable variants. Non-checking builds accept the extra argument and perform no test.

Doubly linked updates initialize new links privately, then publish the predecessor forward link with release ordering and finally repair the successor back link, after an add-validity test. Head and tail insertion select the appropriate neighbors. Removal unlinks and marks the old back link as poisoned in one variant while leaving it unmarked in the bidirectional variant. Replacement and splicing follow the same publish-then-repair order, with empty-source checks skipping the splice and init variants reinitializing the source.

Hash-list updates link a new node privately, publish through the predecessor pointer with release ordering, and repair the successor back link. Insertion supports head, tail by linear walk, before a successor, and behind a predecessor. Deletion unlinks and either poisons or nulls the back pointer depending on variant. Replacement preserves the successor chain and poisons the old node. Swapping two heads exchanges first pointers and repairs both back links.

Bit-locked insertion assumes the bucket lock is held, links the new node against the current first node using plain accesses, then publishes the locked first word with release ordering. Deletion unlinks and poisons the back pointer. Publishing the first word requires the new node to carry no lock bits and the head to be in locked state, preserving the lock bit in the stored value.
Nulls-terminated deletion checks whether the node is hashed and only then unlinks it and clears its back pointer to null, leaving unhashed nodes untouched.

Removed or replaced nodes carry poison markers and must not be dereferenced or re-traversed until after a grace period; unmarked bidirectional removal relies on external exclusion instead. Backward links must not be traversed concurrently with splicing that reinitializes the source. Head swapping requires both lists to be non-empty. Tail insertion by walking is writer-side only and must exclude concurrent writers.

Splicing with reinitialization follows a three-phase protocol. First the source is reset to empty with reader-safe initialization so new readers observe emptiness. Then a caller-supplied blocking wait drains pre-existing readers of the old body under exclusive access. Finally the detached body is linked into its new position with release publication of the predecessor link.

Splice-with-reinit variants require the caller to provide a synchronization callback that blocks until all pre-existing readers have finished, and to hold exclusive ownership of the transferred first and last links across that wait. Plain splice has no wait and relies on external writer exclusion.
Each routed header defines a unique include-once guard macro, ensuring repeated inclusion within a translation unit contributes its declarations a single time.
The splice-with-reinit helpers accept a caller-provided no-argument blocking function that is invoked synchronously between source reset and destination linking to wait out pre-existing readers.
